documents.title: Guidelines for Using Generative Artificial Intelligence in Instructional Settings at UCR
documents.summary: The Provost's September 2025 guidelines give six principles (beneficial use, equity, information security, local authority, accountability, transparency) and suggested practices for instructors. Instructors decide whether and how students use AI; the document stresses secure tools, clear syllabus statements, assessment redesign and caution about detectors.
documents.stance_why: Principle 4 says 'the Instructor of Record has broad latitude to determine whether and how generative AI may be used', and the practices tell instructors to 'Establish clear expectations in your syllabus'. The document sets no default allow or ban, so it delegates.

units.why: The sentence frames the document as a 'foundational resource for responsibly integrating' AI, so it is an institution-wide framework (P56) stating purpose and scope, addressed to everyone (all) as a general principle.
units.anchor: a foundational resource for responsibly integrating these powerful tools into instructional settings

units.why: 'UCR is committed to equipping our students, faculty, and staff with the knowledge and skills to appropriately and effectively utilize generative AI' states the university will teach effective AI use as a skill; closest is P44 (professional skill) though it also reads as a training commitment (P70).
units.anchor: committed to equipping our students, faculty, and staff with the knowledge and skills
units.fit_note: Framed as an institutional commitment to equip all members, not only a course-level professional-skill claim; also resembles training provision (P70).

units.why: Principle 1 says any use 'should aim to improve the learning experience' and position students for success. It ties AI use to learning outcomes, nearest P83, but it names no learning objectives, so it fits only partly.
units.anchor: should aim to improve the learning experience for students
units.fit_note: Asks that AI use improve learning and future success generally; does not mention course or program learning objectives.

units.why: 'Students must have equal access to generative AI tools when used in instructional settings' is an equity rule: access must be equal when AI is part of instruction. It binds instructors and units that deploy AI, so actor is all; type P51.
units.anchor: Students must have equal access to generative AI tools when used in instructional settings.

units.why: 'Anything that is uploaded to a publicly available AI tool effectively enters the public domain' is a factual warning about data exposure that underlies the privacy rules; informs, privacy type P50.
units.anchor: Anything that is uploaded to a publicly available AI tool effectively enters the public domain.

units.why: Tools that 'have not passed a campus security review may be used with public data only' limits what data may go into unvetted AI tools. It is a data-protection and vetted-tool rule (P50) rather than a review process (P65).
units.anchor: may be used with public data only

units.why: 'UCR provides access to secure tools including Google Gemini and Microsoft Copilot' names institution-wide approved tools for sensitive data. It is university-wide, not course-specific, so P92 not P17.
units.anchor: UCR provides access to secure tools including Google Gemini and Microsoft Copilot.

units.why: 'the Instructor of Record has broad latitude to determine whether and how generative AI may be used' hands the decision to instructors, the core of P04 and the reason the document is coded delegates.
units.anchor: provided this use is consistent with applicable policies and rules governing data security

units.why: The latitude applies only 'provided this use is consistent with applicable policies and rules governing data security and instruction', i.e. instructor choices must comply with existing policy (P77); this is separate from the latitude itself (P04).
units.anchor: provided this use is consistent with applicable policies and rules governing data security

units.why: 'Not all generative AI responses are accurate' warns that AI output can be wrong; students and others are expected to be aware of it, so P31 as an informs statement.
units.anchor: Not all generative AI responses are accurate
units.fit_note: States that output can be inaccurate but does not explicitly instruct users to verify it.

units.why: 'some may violate intellectual property rights' names an IP risk of AI output; informs, P52.
units.anchor: some may violate intellectual property rights

units.why: 'perpetuate biases inherent in model design and/or training datasets' names bias as a concern about AI; informs, P53.
units.anchor: may perpetuate biases inherent in model design and/or training datasets

units.why: 'Anyone using generative AI for any purpose is accountable for the consequences of their use' makes users answerable for what they produce. P29 (own what you submit) is nearest; it is broader than submitted work.
units.anchor: Anyone using generative AI for any purpose is accountable for the consequences of their use
units.fit_note: Accountability for consequences of any AI use by anyone, not only ownership of submitted student work.

units.why: Accountability 'includes but is not limited to violations of academic integrity policies, other institutional policies and rules, and applicable laws'; it says AI use falls under existing policies and law, which is P77.
units.anchor: violations of academic integrity policies, other institutional policies and rules, and applicable laws

units.why: Principle 6 says anyone using AI 'must conform with prevailing ethical scholarship practices, rules related to plagiarism, and standards for representing intellectual products as one's own work'. This applies existing rules to AI (P45 nearest) and implies attribution without naming disclosure.
units.anchor: must conform with prevailing ethical scholarship practices, rules related to plagiarism
units.fit_note: Applies existing plagiarism and scholarship rules to AI use but does not compare AI to a human collaborator and does not explicitly require disclosure.

units.why: The suggested practice 'Be mindful of security and privacy issues' tells instructors to follow AI security and privacy practices; it is a data-protection rule, P50.
units.anchor: Adhering to AI security and privacy practices is vital to protecting UCR

units.why: 'Explore the capabilities of generative AI by logging into your UCR account and experimenting' urges instructors to learn AI before setting policy; this is faculty support/learning, P63.
units.anchor: Explore the capabilities of generative AI by logging into your UCR account

units.why: 'UCR has established contractual agreements with Google for its AI tools, which offer enhanced security and privacy' states that the university-provided tool is safer; it supports use of approved tools (P92).
units.anchor: UCR has established contractual agreements with Google for its AI tools

units.why: Instructors are told AI 'can draft or revise sections of your syllabus, create lesson plans, summarize readings' and similar tasks. This lists permitted instructor uses of AI in teaching work, P59.
units.anchor: can draft or revise sections of your syllabus, create lesson plans, summarize readings

units.why: 'analyze spreadsheet data to identify trends in student performance, and provide personalized feedback' suggests instructors use AI to analyze data and give feedback; feedback and teaching work, P59 (feedback conditions P101 are not stated).
units.anchor: analyze spreadsheet data to identify trends in student performance, and provide personalized feedback

units.why: 'Consider how students can utilize generative AI, consistent with your course standards' invites instructors to decide student uses, again leaving the rule to the course (P04).
units.anchor: Consider how students can utilize generative AI, consistent with your course standards.

units.why: AI 'can help students brainstorm topics for a writing assignment' and create outlines; this lists brainstorming as a student use instructors may allow (P15).
units.anchor: can help students brainstorm topics for a writing assignment
units.frag_start: Generative AI can enrich the student

units.why: AI can 'summarize research articles or class notes' and 'generate practice problems', which are study-aid uses (P14); same sentence as brainstorming but a distinct permitted use.
units.anchor: summarize research articles or class notes, create presentation outlines, and generate practice problems

units.why: The practice asks instructors to 'Consider implementing authentic assessment methods', listing case studies, portfolios, oral exams and similar; assessments are redesigned around AI (P35).
units.anchor: Consider implementing authentic assessment methods in your course.
units.fit_note: Suggests authentic methods (also naming oral exams, P34) that include the use of generative AI in the real world.

units.why: 'If you choose to keep more traditional assessment methods, think carefully about the implications of generative AI' tells instructors to restructure assessment conditions or outcomes; assessment redesign, P35.
units.anchor: You may need to change the outcomes you are assessing and/or the conditions
units.frag_start: If you choose to keep more

units.why: 'XCITE offers resources and workshops to help you explore the possibilities' names support for instructors learning about AI (P63).
units.anchor: XCITE offers resources and workshops to help you explore the possibilities.

units.why: Instructors are asked to 'achieve some degree of alignment of your course standards with those of your immediate colleagues' for department-level consistency. No type covers aligning course rules with colleagues, so UNCOVERED rather than P85 (units set own rules).
units.anchor: achieve some degree of alignment of your course standards with those of your immediate colleagues
units.uncovered_note: Instructors should try to align their course AI standards with colleagues in the department so students see consistency.

units.why: 'Establish clear expectations in your syllabus' tells instructors to put AI expectations in the syllabus: P09.
units.anchor: Establish clear expectations in your syllabus
units.frag_end: document the use of generative AI in their work.

units.why: The same sentence says the syllabus should state 'how students should cite and document the use of generative AI'; this is an instructor duty to set a disclosure and citation expectation (P24).
units.anchor: how students should cite and document the use of generative AI in their work
units.frag_start: Establish clear expectations in your syllabus
units.fit_note: Instructors are told to specify how students cite; the document does not itself require disclosure.

units.why: 'Also establish clear expectations for each assessment' asks for assignment-level AI expectations to avoid integrity problems; closest type is P09 (state expectations), applied per assessment.
units.anchor: establish clear expectations for each assessment to help avoid potential problems related to academic
units.frag_start: Also establish clear expectations for each

units.why: 'If you suspect academic misconduct, follow the standard campus procedures' tells instructors to use the formal integrity process, P81.
units.anchor: If you suspect academic misconduct, follow the standard campus procedures

units.why: 'automated AI detection tools can be inaccurate and prone to bias' warns against trusting detectors, P39.
units.anchor: automated AI detection tools can be inaccurate and prone to bias
units.frag_start: keep in mind that automated AI
units.fit_note: Cautions instructors that detectors are inaccurate; it does not say they must not be used.

units.why: 'Share your own ideas about generative AI with your students, including how you are using it in your research and teaching' asks instructors to tell students about their own AI use (P47).
units.anchor: over-reliance on generative AI can undermine their education, opportunities for intellectual growth
units.fit_note: Also invites sharing views about AI generally, not only disclosure of the instructor's own use.

units.why: 'Remind students that over-reliance on generative AI can undermine their education' gives a reason instructors should relay: AI use can weaken learning and exam or interview performance (P43 false mastery nearest).
units.anchor: over-reliance on generative AI can undermine their education, opportunities for intellectual growth
units.fit_note: Warns that over-reliance undermines education and later performance in exams and interviews; does not use the idea of a false sense of mastery.

units.why: 'contact the library at libteaching@ucr.edu' for student resources on ethical and responsible AI use sends instructors and students to human support (P72).
units.anchor: please contact the library at libteaching@ucr.edu.
units.frag_start: If you would like resources for students

documents.unit: Vice Chancellor for Student Affairs (student mailing list)
documents.title: [Students] Update on Artificial Intelligence Use
documents.summary: A 2023 email from the Vice Chancellor for Student Affairs to students. It urges checking with professors, using AI to assist and not replace original work, citing AI use, protecting privacy, and warns of academic-integrity penalties; it lists support offices.
documents.stance_why: The email tells students to 'discuss with your professors for specific policies' and to 'Follow the guidance of your professors'. Its only own rule, not generating deliverables 'in their entirety', is soft ('should not'), so the decision stays with instructors: delegates.

units.why: 'We encourage you to discuss with your professors for specific policies or expectations before engaging in the use of Generative AI' tells students to check with instructors before using AI: P10.
units.anchor: discuss with your professors for specific policies or expectations before engaging in the use

units.why: 'Using AI tools should assist or enhance, not replace, your original work' makes AI an aid and bans replacing the student's own work, which is P32 (student stays the primary thinker).
units.anchor: Using AI tools should assist or enhance, not replace, your original work.

units.why: 'you should not use it to generate essays, assignments, or other deliverables in their entirety' forbids having AI produce the whole submission (P19), with soft modality 'should not'.
units.anchor: you should not use it to generate essays, assignments, or other deliverables in their entirety
units.fit_note: Bans only generating whole deliverables; partial AI help is left open.

units.why: 'AI can assist with data analysis' says students may use AI for data analysis, P89.
units.anchor: AI can assist with data analysis
units.frag_start: Get familiar with generative AI before using

units.why: AI can 'generate ideas, or help structure your thoughts' states idea generation and outlining as acceptable uses (P15 brainstorming).
units.anchor: generate ideas, or help structure your thoughts

units.why: 'Your work should reflect your understanding, thoughts, and efforts' says submitted work must reflect the student's own understanding, P29.
units.anchor: Your work should reflect your understanding, thoughts, and efforts.

units.why: 'Follow the guidance of your professors for specific policies or expectations' tells students to follow each course's AI rules, P78. It recurs in two bullets; coded once here.
units.anchor: Follow the guidance of your professors for specific policies or expectations

units.why: 'If you use AI-generated content or data ... ensure that you cite it properly' requires attribution of AI use: P24.
units.anchor: If you use AI-generated content or data as part of your research

units.why: 'extremely difficult to verify the quality of the information in their responses' warns that AI gives no sources so output is hard to check; P31 verify.
units.anchor: may not provide you with the citations from where they are generating their responses

units.why: 'AI can produce responses that are not always accurate and/or may violate intellectual property rights' warns students about errors and IP; the error part is P31.
units.anchor: AI can produce responses that are not always accurate

units.why: 'They also may perpetuate biases inherent in their design and/or training datasets' names bias, P53.
units.anchor: may perpetuate biases inherent in their design and/or training datasets

units.why: 'Avoid sharing personal or sensitive information' with AI tools is a data-protection instruction to students, P50.
units.anchor: Avoid sharing personal or sensitive information.

units.why: 'Always ensure that the software or platform you're using is from a reputable source and has adequate security measures' tells students to choose vetted tools, P50.
units.anchor: ensure that the software or platform

units.why: 'be wary of freely available online AI tools that may not have clearly stated privacy policies' warns against tools with unclear data practices, P50.

units.why: 'ranging from receiving a failing grade for the assignment to more severe academic penalties' states concrete penalties in advance, P37.

units.why: 'honesty and integrity are fundamental educational and community values' grounds AI rules in integrity as a community value, P95.
units.anchor: honesty and integrity are fundamental educational and community values

units.why: The email lists the Academic Resource Center, Writing and Reading Support, library and conduct office as UCR resources 'to bolster student research, learning' with AI; it points students to human help, P72.
